name: Comparative Lit (PhD)

children.desc: Required all years: Enrollment in COMPLIT 397 (Graduate Studies Colloquium) is required each quarter that the student is in the program from year 1 to graduation, including while on TGR Status, except when conducting research away from campus or on an approved leave of absence. Participation in the Colloquium is a part of each student’s annual review.
children.name: Graduate Studies Colloquium (COMPLIT 397, every quarter)

rules.name: Courses in Primary Field
rules.desc: At least six courses in the student’s primary field must be taken to ensure knowledge of the essential works in one national literature from its beginnings to the present.

rules.name: Complementary Courses
rules.desc: At least four additional courses must be taken, with most of the reading in the original, in two different national literatures (i.e., two courses in each literature).

First-Year Colloquium
All first-year students participate in the Comparative Literature First-Year Colloquium, which takes place in mid-May. At the First-Year Colloquium, each student offers an oral presentation of 20-30 minutes on a literary text, followed by up to 30 minutes of discussion. The assessment is based on engagement with the text, the interpretive framework (theoretical, historical, etc.), and the quality of argument of the presentation. The First-Year Colloquium is a public event. A student whose performance is deemed insufficient may schedule a second presentation during the first week of the Autumn quarter of the second year. See the DLCL Graduate Handbook for more information.
Qualifying Paper
Students who succeed in the First Year Colloquium proceed to the second milestone: submission of a Qualifying Paper by May 1 of the second year.
rules.name: First-Year Colloquium and Qualifying Paper
Prospectus Colloquium
rules.desc: The Prospectus Colloquium normally takes place the quarter after the University Oral Exam (winter quarter of year three). See the DLCL Graduate Handbook for details.
Although teaching is not a requirement for the degree, students may teach as part of the financial support commitment and their professional training.

Students are expected to follow department qualifying procedures and apply for candidacy by the end of the second year in residence. In reviewing a student for admission to candidacy, the faculty considers a student’s academic progress, including but not limited to:

• Demonstrated proficiency in three languages as defined in the handbook.

• Performance in courses and completion of required coursework

• Performance on departmental examinations and milestones, including the First Year-Colloquium presentation and the Qualifying Paper.

• Completion of at least three units of work with each of four Stanford faculty members
Proficiency in languages will be formally assessed during graduate study and must be certified before admission to candidacy by examination administered through the Stanford Language Center.
In addition to successfully completing departmental requirements for years one and two, a student is only admitted to candidacy if the faculty makes the judgment that the student has the potential to complete the degree program requirements successfully. Candidacy is determined by faculty vote. Failure to be admitted to candidacy results in the student’s dismissal from the Ph.D. program.
rules.name: Advancement to candidacy
Three languages (your native language, advanced proficiency in a second, intermediate in a third), certified by examination by spring of year 2

rules.desc: The University Oral Examinations in Comparative Literature covers a literary period of about a century in three or more literatures with primary emphasis on a single national literature or, in occasional cases, two national literatures. The reading list, which should be determined through consultation with the examiners and the Department Director, chiefly covers the major literary texts of a period of approximately one hundred years, normally in three different language traditions, but may also include some studies of intellectual backgrounds and modern critical discussions of the period. Students are expected to complete this milestone by week 9 of the Autumn quarter of their third year of the program. See the Graduate Handbook for more information.
rules.name: University Oral Examination

rules.desc: The dissertation may take different formats. The standard format in our field is a monograph comprising five chapters, including the introduction and conclusion. Depending on the topic and approach, other formats may be considered and should be discussed with the advisor as the project develops. In consultation with their advisor, students may elect to submit as a dissertation a collection of three to four published, or publishable, articles, together with an introduction. Students are expected to submit the dissertation by the end of their fifth year in the program.
rules.name: Dissertation
Language Requirement
rules.desc:
Students must demonstrate competence in three languages in total.
One of these is the student’s native language. Students must achieve advanced proficiency in the second language. For the third language, intermediate proficiency is required. Language requirements must be satisfied by Spring of year two.
One of the student’s three literatures/languages is usually designated as the primary field, the other two as secondary. However, some students may designate two primary literatures (by completing six or more graduate courses in that literature). See the DLCL Graduate Handbook for more information.
Proficiency in languages will be formally assessed during graduate study and must be certified before admission to candidacy by examination administered through the Stanford Language Center.

grading:
All courses counted toward the 135-unit requirement for the PhD must be at the graduate level. At least three consecutive quarters of coursework must be taken at Stanford.
Ph.D. students in the department must take required courses for a letter grade if available, and they are expected to earn a grade of B+ or better in each course taken. Any grade of B or below is considered to be less than satisfactory. Grades of B or below are reviewed by faculty, and the following actions may be taken:

• The grade stands, and the student’s academic performance is monitored to ensure that satisfactory progress is being made

• The student may be required to retake the course
The principal conditions for continued registration of a graduate student are the timely and satisfactory completion of the university, department, and program requirements for the degree and fulfillment of minimum progress requirements. Failure to meet these requirements results in corrective measures, including a written warning, and/or the possible dismissal from the program.
transferPolicy: Students who completed graduate coursework at another institution are expected to transfer course units in the winter quarter of their first year of doctoral study. The Department Director will evaluate the transfer of units on a course-by-course basis. Graduate work accepted for transfer of residency does not automatically exempt a student from having to complete a course requirement for the degree.
reviewNotes: The audit checks COMPLIT 346, DLCL 301, DLCL 369 and the COMPLIT 397 colloquium, letter graded where a letter grade is offered, and 135 units in all, counting only graduate-level listings. You check by hand the six primary-field and four complementary courses, the First-Year Colloquium and Qualifying Paper, certification in three languages (your native language, an advanced second and an intermediate third) by spring of your second year, candidacy, the University Oral Exam, the Prospectus Colloquium and the dissertation. A grade of B or below is reviewed by the faculty but does not by itself stop a course from counting.
